name: Classic Steak Tartare

ingredients.name: finely minced flat-leaf parsley leaves, tender stems

instructions.primary_message: On a very clean work surface and using a sharp knife, slice beef into thin slices no thicker than 1/4 inch. Then cut into thin 1/4- or 1/8-inch stips. Cut strips crosswise into a fine mince. Transfer to a mixing bowl.

Add mayonnaise and season with salt and pepper to taste, stirring well to combine thoroughly. If needed add additional olive oil, vinegar, and/or mustard in very small increments to adjust flavor to taste (depending on your mayonnaise, you may not need any, or you may find the beef needs a little more to get the flavor just right). If desired, mix in the drops of fish sauce.
Add shallot, chives, parsley, cornichon, and capers and stir until thoroughly combined.

Mound steak tartare on a serving plate (you can use a ring mold to make a perfect circle, if desired). Top with egg yolk, if using, and serve right away with toasts and additional cornichons on the side.

description: Steak tartare is a bistro classic that we should all be making at home. Here's everything you need to know to do it safely, find the best cuts of beef, and make the dish as delicious as possible.
notes:
Optional or for serving: 1/2 teaspoon Worcestershire sauce or 3 drops fish sauce (optional); 1 teaspoon finely minced cornichons, plus whole cornichons for serving; 1 large egg yolk (optional, see notes); Toasts, for serving

Optional substitutions: Red wine vinegar → white wine vinegar

Notes: If you're especially concerned about food safety but are still determined to eat steak tartare, you can further reduce the chances of illness by searing the whole tenderloin in a smoking hot, lightly oil skillet, making sure to give several seconds of full contact to the hot pan to every surface of the meat; if done quickly and over very high heat, this will kill bacteria on the surface of the meat while leaving the interior of the beef fully raw.
Similarly, you can attempt to pasteurize your eggs at home before topping the tartare with the yolk (and before making the mayonnaise). The whites will thicken and be slightly cloudy after this heat treatment, so just remove them before setting the yolk on the tartare.
Neither process is foolproof, but each is better than doing nothing.
author: Daniel Gritzer
